pages.intro: Savi Saluwadana is a software engineer based in Sri Lanka interested in system architecture, backend and mobile development, distributed systems, cloud-native platforms and agentic AI. His portfolio explores software products across industries, technical writing and engineering experiments.

blocks.text: My professional focus is software engineering and product development: designing application boundaries, building reliable APIs, modelling data and connecting software to real business workflows. Platform engineering and developer experience are part of that broader focus, not my sole professional identity.

My previous internship at WSO2 concluded in November 2026. It is past experience, not my current employment. This website is my independent professional portfolio and does not list a current employer.

My portfolio work includes independent software projects, technical writing and engineering experiments. See the [project directory](/products/) and [architecture reference](/engineering/) for concrete examples and the scope of each contribution.

My academic background is in software engineering. The following educational and technical qualifications are self-reported; current credential validity and degree completion should be verified with the issuing institutions.

blocks.text: I am interested in the complete lifecycle of software systems: understanding a problem, designing an architecture, building backend services and client applications, and operating reliable systems. My interests span the following areas; they are not claims of expertise in every technology or of production-scale outcomes.

rows: Domain-driven design, modular monoliths, microservices, event-driven systems, architecture trade-offs, integration boundaries and designing systems for maintainability. Explore the [architecture reference](/engineering/).

Go, Rust and TypeScript services; API design, authentication, authorization, concurrency, background workers, transactions, data consistency and caching. Examples: [Property Management OS](/products/property-os/) and [Advance HRIS](/products/advance-hris/).

Cross-platform applications with Flutter and React Native, mobile-first product design, offline-first data, notifications, synchronization and secure integration with backend services. These are development interests, not a claim that every technology is used in a shipped app.

Fault tolerance, distributed coordination, messaging, idempotency, observability, performance testing and recovery from partial failures. See [durable agentic workflows](/insights/durable-agentic-workflows/).
Building web and mobile experiences around real user workflows, from prototypes to maintainable products. Explore [Avara](/products/avara/) and [FreshPick](/products/freshpick/).

Containers, Kubernetes, infrastructure automation, CI/CD, developer platforms, deployment reliability and developer experience. See [platform engineering paved roads](/insights/platform-engineering-paved-road/).

Relational modelling, PostgreSQL, data pipelines, event processing, search and retrieval, storage and multi-tenant data isolation. See [PostgreSQL multi-tenancy](/insights/postgres-multitenancy-boundaries/).
Tool-using agents, MCP, orchestration, retrieval, agent evaluation, permissions and human-in-the-loop systems. Explore [agentic systems architecture](/engineering/agentic-systems/).
Understanding real implementations, contributing to public projects, improving documentation and sharing reproducible engineering experiments. Browse the [public repository index](/open-source/).

pages.title: Project Architecture and Design Decisions | Savi Saluwadana
pages.heading: Software architecture across product workflows.
pages.label: Engineering / Architecture reference
pages.description: Inspect project architecture decisions on APIs, data authority, local-first workflows, tenancy and transactions in Savi Saluwadana's software.
pages.intro: A reference to the boundaries behind my product work: where authority lives, how clients access it, and what a workflow actually guarantees. Each comparison links to the relevant product architecture and current scope.

sections.title: AI agents and MCP access boundaries

blocks.text: Model Context Protocol gives an agent a tool interface. The useful architectural question is what happens behind that interface: which service authorizes the request, where reasoning runs, and whether an action needs approval.

rows: MCP calls the same authenticated Go HTTP API used by other clients. Domain rules and tenant permissions remain server-side; the MCP server has no direct database connection.
The local Next.js dashboard calls a Rust API backed by PostgreSQL. The repository also has a separate desktop edition with its own capabilities.

blocks.text: These are different boundaries. An agent tool does not imply unrestricted writes or an autonomous production workflow. Product scope notes describe the implemented tools, provider configuration and evidence requirements. The [agentic systems walkthroughs](/engineering/agentic-systems/) follow each request through its tool, service and recorded state.

[Advance HRIS](/products/advance-hris/) combines a Next.js web application with a Wails/React desktop console, encrypted SQLite payloads and a sync queue. The Go API and cloud PostgreSQL database remain authoritative. The local-first boundary belongs to the desktop workflow.

[NexusPOS](/products/nexus-pos/) has an optional Electron desktop shell around the retail application. Desktop packaging alone does not establish an offline checkout engine. That distinction matters when evaluating a product for disconnected operations.
To assess a local-first system, identify the authoritative record, the queued work, and the conflict-resolution boundary. A local database or desktop executable answers only part of that question.

A SaaS interface and a tenant-isolated backend are separate architectural concerns. [Property Management OS](/products/property-os/) documents multi-tenant rental operations, role-based access and domain rules in its Go API. [Acme Accounting](/products/acme-accounting/) currently uses one company and one administrator identity per database.

[Academix](/products/academix/) has role-aware academic workflows and SaaS plan surfaces, while broader tenant-isolation and automated-billing work remain subject to its roadmap. The product labels should be read together with the current implementation boundaries.

The reference point is the server-side rule: who can read or change a record, which organization owns it, and which transaction maintains its integrity. A dashboard or plan selector does not establish those guarantees by itself.

sections.title: Bookings, recurring orders and payment workflows

rows: Property and booking workflows connect to PayHere payment callbacks and S3 media. Payment and storage integrations need deployment-specific configuration.
Next.js and PostgreSQL support food commerce and scheduled recurring delivery. Checkout and subscription baskets currently use cash on delivery; automatic recurring card charging is not implemented.
Matching and event procurement use a Next.js/PostgreSQL application. Payment evidence is submitted and reconciled manually in the current MVP.

blocks.text: A booking, a recurring order and a payment represent different state changes. Keeping those boundaries explicit makes the architecture easier to inspect and prevents a delivery schedule from being mistaken for automated billing.

pages.name: Agentic systems architecture
pages.title: Project Agent Interfaces and Workflow Boundaries | Savi Saluwadana
pages.heading: Agentic systems: tools, state and human review.
pages.label: Engineering / Agentic systems
pages.description: Inspect agent tool boundaries, application permissions and local research workflows documented in Savi Saluwadana's projects.
pages.intro: An agent becomes useful when its tools connect to a real workflow. These project walkthroughs show where an agent enters the system, where state is recorded, and which service controls the resulting action.

blocks.text: The model, tool interface and domain service have different responsibilities. The model can propose an action, while the application still needs to determine whether that action is permitted and what record it changes. The examples below expose those boundaries rather than treating every AI feature as the same architecture.

rows: MCP tools call the authenticated Go API.
Organization scope and domain rules remain in the API. PostgreSQL stores business records and notification intents.
A connected MCP host performs semantic research and synthesis.
The Rust API records evidence and research state in PostgreSQL; research findings still need validation. The application does not call model APIs directly.
Gemini assists with summaries after CSV analysis.
Threshold logic computes flags. Account connectors are mocks, so this prototype is not a durable live-account ingestion system.

blocks.text: In [Property Management OS](/products/property-os/), an agent uses the same authenticated HTTP boundary as another client. Adding a tool interface does not create an alternative route around tenant permissions or domain rules.

The recorded domain operation and notification delivery have separate responsibilities. The database holds the record and notification intent; an outbox worker performs delivery through a configured provider. That separation is useful when inspecting whether a business action was accepted versus whether its notification was delivered.

The documented MCP scope matters: advanced financial writes and other domains should be checked against the implemented tools. The existence of an API endpoint is not evidence that an agent has permission to perform every operation.

[Pain Intelligence Lab](/products/pain-intelligence/) separates host reasoning from the application that stores research evidence. A question becomes a research job; the host gathers and annotates evidence through tools while the application retains the project state.

The output is evaluated as evidence, not just generated text. Source diversity, duplicate checks, independent stories and competitor or pricing validation affect whether an opportunity survives the research process. A job can correctly finish with no validated opportunity.

This boundary also changes how the system is configured: the connected host provides semantic reasoning, while the platform provides storage, inspection and quality checks. Model-provider behavior should not be inferred from the Rust API alone.
An agent can propose a change without being authorized to execute it. Keep consequential actions behind application permissions and explicit human review.

For the design rationale, read [Durable Agentic Workflows](/insights/durable-agentic-workflows/) and [MCP Permission Boundaries](/insights/mcp-permission-boundaries/). These are design notes, not claims of measured production outcomes.

For practical runtime design, read [AI Agent Harness Architecture](/insights/ai-agent-harness-architecture/), [The Bounded Agent Loop](/insights/bounded-agent-loop/) and [Evaluating AI Agents](/insights/agent-evaluation-observability/). These notes cover control boundaries, termination and repeatable outcome checks.

sections.title: What I want to develop further

blocks.text: My broader interests include durable orchestration, multi-agent collaboration, retrieval and evaluation. The following are design questions I want to explore, rather than claims that every project already implements the same capabilities.

items: How should a tool make repeated requests safe when an agent or worker retries?
Which state should persist so a long-running task can resume after failure?
How can agents share evidence and responsibilities without losing provenance?
What evaluation catches unauthorized actions, weak evidence and incorrect outcomes before they reach a user?
Which actions need human review, and how should that decision be recorded?

pages.intro: EventMesh is event experience software in development for conferences, meetups and exhibitions. It explores how attendees can find relevant people, topics and sessions, arrange conversations and record useful outcomes.

blocks.text: Large events create a discovery problem: attendees have limited time and incomplete information about sessions, projects and people. EventMesh explores a structured way to connect attendee intent to relevant event opportunities.

rows: A Next.js interface for attendee and event workflows.
Application APIs, business rules, event-scoped access and booking operations.
Authoritative event, membership and reservation data.

items: Match attendees to relevant event opportunities using explicit criteria and deterministic ranking.
Protect booking capacity and prevent duplicate reservations under concurrent requests.
Keep private attendee data and event-scoped permissions separate.
Explore real-time state delivery and recoverable event updates.
Design mobile-friendly event interactions for short, time-constrained journeys.

blocks.text: See [Go modular monolith architecture](/insights/go-modular-monolith-saas/) and [PostgreSQL multi-tenancy](/insights/postgres-multitenancy-boundaries/) for related engineering approaches.

pages.name: Engineering Lab
pages.title: Interactive Engineering Lab | Savi Saluwadana
pages.heading: Engineering laboratory
pages.label: Engineering / Reproducible models
pages.description: Run interactive models of idempotent retries, concurrent reservations and agent authorization. Inspect invariants, traces and limitations.
pages.intro: Explore three small, deterministic software engineering models. Change inputs, compare unsafe and protected designs, and inspect the resulting decisions. These are educational simulations, not production benchmarks or measured service performance.

blocks.text: At-least-once delivery may send the same request more than once. Compare a handler that applies every request with one that remembers processed request identities. The invariant is exactly one side effect per unique request.
Try five requests with two retries. With deduplication, 15 deliveries produce five effects and ten suppressed replays. Without it, 15 effects are applied.

The model uses an in-memory set, not an atomic database transaction. Production code must address persistence, transaction boundaries, concurrent claims and the retention lifetime of idempotency keys. Read [durable agentic workflows](/insights/durable-agentic-workflows/).

A check-then-write race can occur when all contenders read the same available capacity before any update becomes visible. Compare that deliberately unsafe schedule with serialized capacity checks and writes. The invariant is that accepted reservations never exceed capacity.
Try three seats and eight contenders. The unsafe schedule accepts eight and oversells by five; the serialized model accepts three and rejects five.

This is an abstract worst-case interleaving, not a concurrent database benchmark. Real implementations need transactional locking or conditional writes, retry handling and isolation testing. See [EventMesh](/projects/eventmesh/) for related architectural concerns.

An agent request must be authorized by application policy, not by the model's intention. In this simplified policy, viewers can read, operators can read and write, and admins can also transfer after human approval. Cross-tenant operations are always denied.
Try an admin transfer with and without approval, or any cross-tenant action. The decision trace exposes each policy check; all checks must pass.

This teaching model omits real identity verification, resource-level permissions, approval expiration and replay protection. It is not a security library. Read [MCP permission boundaries](/insights/mcp-permission-boundaries/).

The browser and automated tests use the same pure JavaScript models. Inspect the [model source](/lab/models.mjs), [test source](/lab/models.test.mjs) and [portfolio repository](https://github.com/savisaluwadana/savisaluwadana.github.io). From a local clone with Node.js 22, run node --test lab/models.test.mjs.

Tests cover bounded inputs, protected and deliberately unsafe cases, and role/action/tenant/approval combinations. These tests establish properties of the simplified models only. Real-service throughput, latency, recovery and distributed failure experiments remain separate work.
